text: Learning areas it should not enter.
Turn off the main water shutoff valve.
Turn off the main electrical breaker.
Unlock and open a window specifically for emergency egress.
Clear a path for emergency medical personnel.
Sharpen knives using a whetstone or pull-through sharpener.
Operate high-risk manual kitchen tools (e.g., mandoline slicer, box grater) without damaging the tool or the robot's end-effectors.
Provide a stable, locked-joint physical brace for a person attempting to stand up or sit down.

Guide a visually impaired person through a cluttered room (acting as a sighted guide).Caring for people (must-have). Most entries are about objects and rooms. People mostly show up as obstacles or as someone to hand things to.
Sick-day care: take a temperature, bring fluids, tissues, and a heating pad, clean up after vomiting, fetch an inhaler or EpiPen, bring medication on the person's own schedule and log it.

Kids: bedtime routine (bath-water temperature check, pajamas, story, night light, checking on a sleeping child), bottle and formula prep, sterilizing, supervised play (catch, hide-and-seek, card and board games), reading aloud.
Answer the doorbell or intercom; screen visitors and decline solicitors; let in expected guests; supervise repair people; accept and sign for deliveries.

Primitives: communication is thin (you have Report, Alert, and Ask for clarification). Add Speak, Listen, Announce, Explain, Confirm, Refuse, Undo, Hand off to a human, Remember, Forget. Physical verbs also missing: Cut/Slice, Peel, Crack, Tear, Hammer, Drill, Climb, Kneel/Crouch, Balance, Throw/Catch, Point/Gesture, Spray, Brush.

text: Repairs: paint walls and touch up scuffs, caulk a tub or sink, patch small holes, sand, regrout, pressure-wash, seal a deck.

Charge or swap its own battery; wipe its cameras and sensors; get up after a fall; wait in an unobtrusive spot; quiet and privacy modes (cameras and mics off in bathrooms and bedrooms); knock before entering an occupied room; ask for remote help; log its own faults.

Technique: carve, fillet, shuck; awkward produce (squash, pineapple, mango, coconut); baking steps (grease and line pans, proof dough, cool on racks, frost); grilling (light, flip, check temperature, propane level); disposing of cooking oil; espresso with steamed milk, pour-over.

Vehicles, bikes, and errands (only if scope goes past the property line). Refuel, check and inflate tires, top off washer fluid, change wipers, jump-start, change a flat, scrape ice and snow, check the back seat before locking, check a car seat; lube a bike chain, patch a flat, charge an e-bike; curbside pickup, pharmacy, post office, donation and return drop-offs.
“Get this out of here.” It must determine whether that means trash it, relocate it, store it, return it, or simply move it to another room.
“Set this room up for a party.” Number of guests, seating, food locations, walking paths, decorations, trash locations, and breakable objects all matter.
“Do the important stuff first.” Requires ranking chores by urgency and impact.
“Check whether I left anything out.” Requires understanding what the expected household state normally looks like.
“Pack everything we might need.” The opposite objective, requiring uncertainty management.
“Cook this without using the oven because it’s broken.” Requires replanning using different appliances.
“Watch this while it cooks.” It has to understand visual, temperature, smell, texture, and timing cues rather than just a timer.
“Cut these into roughly equal pieces.” Requires estimating volume, not simply following a predefined cut pattern.
“Make this easier for a kid to eat.” Requires contextual food preparation and safety judgment.
“Find something I can stand this on.” Requires assessing stability and load.
“Figure out how to open this.” The container may have a mechanism the robot has never encountered.
“Get this sofa around the corner.” A classic high-dimensional geometry and coordination problem.
“Move this upstairs.” Requires judging weight, balance, stair geometry, grip opportunities, and whether human assistance is necessary.
“Leave the important stuff.” Requires distinguishing importance contextually.
“Figure out why the floor is wet.” Could be spilled water, a leak, pet water, rain, appliance overflow, etc.
“Something is leaking. Find it.” Requires tracing evidence to a source.
“There’s a weird noise somewhere.” Requires localization, appliance knowledge, and anomaly detection.
“Check whether anything changed since I left.” Requires storing and comparing previous environmental states.
“Prepare the backyard for people.” Requires inspecting and deciding what matters: seating, debris, shade, toys, wet surfaces, pet waste, etc.
“Clean up after the storm.” Requires adapting to unpredictable debris and possibly unsafe conditions.
“Bring in anything valuable.” Requires semantic judgment about value.
“Make this safe for the dog.” Requires pet-specific hazard reasoning.
“Open the door for the delivery person but keep the pets inside.” Multi-agent dynamic reasoning.
“Grab something that will work instead.” Requires tool substitution.
“Figure out why this appliance isn’t turning on.” Requires safe diagnostic reasoning while knowing when not to proceed.
“If you’re not sure, find another way.” Requires generating alternative plans rather than freezing.
“Get rid of the junk.” Very difficult because one person's junk may be another person's valuable possession.
“Use your best judgment.” The robot has to choose without explicit procedural instruction.
“Figure it out.” Possibly the ultimate generalization benchmark: inspect state, infer intent, construct a plan, act, detect failure, recover, and know when to ask for help.

“Catch this falling object.” Requires dynamic reflexive control, predicting the trajectory of an object in freefall, and deciding whether it is safe to catch (e.g., catching a falling cup vs. letting a falling knife hit the floor).

“We’re out of paper towels; find something else to clean this up.” The robot must evaluate the nature of the spill (oil, water, biohazard) and find a suitable, safe alternative (a rag, a sponge, newspaper) without ruining a nice towel.
“Keep the kids busy for ten minutes.” The robot must invent a safe, engaging game using only the objects currently available in the room.
“Don't let anyone into the garage but me.” Requires persistent facial/voice recognition and the ability to politely refuse commands from unauthorized humans.
“Open the door for that man.” or “Give me the knife.” (from a child) Requires deciding who can command what, refusing without escalating, and alerting an adult.
“The toilet’s overflowing — do something!” Requires improvising a response (shutoff valve, float, towels) with no named procedure.
“Keep an eye on the kids while I shower.” Requires deciding what to watch for, when to intervene, and when to come get me.
“Reach the top shelf.” Requires choosing a stool, reacher, or ladder, or asking for help.
“Learn the house.” Requires mapping rooms, objects, owners, no-go zones, shutoff locations, and the emergency plan, including in a home that isn’t yours.
“Clean it without bleach — the baby’s crawling.” Requires substituting methods under a new constraint.
